newsitem.title: GERMANY: North German metal pay talks break down.
newsitem.headline: North German metal pay talks break down.

text.p: Talks between metal and engineering unions and employers in the north German region of kueste broke down in the early hours of Wednesday with no agreement reached on the issue of sick pay cuts.

After 15 hours of discussions the negotiation leaders, debating wages for 190,000 workers, said talks would continue on Thursday and said they had only reached an agreement over job protection measures, leaving aside the disputed issue of the balance of overtime.
Frank Teichmueller, head of the IG Metall trade union in the region, said he had presented the employers in the region with the annulation of wage agreements for Hamburg and Schleswig-Holstein.
Teichmueller said Thursday would be the last chance to avoid threatened strikes.
The negotiation leaders said the sticking point in their discussions had been the dispute over sick pay cuts and how it had been resolved in the state of Lower Saxony.
A break-through deal was signed last week in Lower Saxony in which metal and engineering employers agreed not to implement a controversial new law cutting sick pay entitlements by 20 percent.
The negotiators said the breakdown of talks had not been sparked by material questions, but rather because of the political significance of the topic.
The employers accused IG Metall of bringing a matter into the talks which had never been discussed in the Northern region before.
At the beginning of the talks on Tuesday morning both sides had shown willingness to orient themselves to the Lower Saxony agreement.

IG Metall hailed last Thursday's agreement, which itself only applies to the some 90,000 workers in the region, as a break-through after protests that have involved hundreds of thousands of workers in the three-million-strong sector.

Under the Lower Saxony package, workers will receive a 1.5 percent rise in 1997 salaries and a 2.5 percent increase in 1998. In return for maintaining full sick pay, workers have agreed to lower Christmas bonuses.
Negotiations in other regions are also going ahead this week in the central state of Hesse and the large southern region of Bavaria.
In the state of Hesse, employers said before talks due on Wednesday that they could accept an agreement similar to that signed in Lower Saxony.

German engineering employers in part of the southern German region of Baden-Wuerttemberg had said on Monday they would thrash out their own wage agreement for the 300,000 workers there rather than adopt the accord reached in Lower Saxony.
